stories.headline: ICE Officer Charged With Aggravated Assault After Striking Man With Car in Houston
stories.summary:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer, Mario Alberto Morales, was charged Friday with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, the Harris County District Attorney's office said. Prosecutors allege he drove an unmarked vehicle into Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, a Mexican construction worker, on Oct. 10 as Parra Hernandez ran away. Parra Hernandez suffered a broken leg and was later taken into custody.

Few federal officers have faced criminal charges for field conduct during the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, which makes the case unusual. District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, said surveillance footage contradicts ICE's account. The video shows an SUV speeding over a median toward Parra Hernandez and ending up inches from him, though another vehicle blocks the view of the impact. ICE has said Parra Hernandez stepped in front of the car and has called the accusations of intentional ramming false and reckless.

Other parts of the ICE account have been questioned. ICE said the target of the operation was Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, but a Houston immigrant rights group said his daughter reported he died in 2017, and Parra Hernandez's family said they never knew him. Teare said DHS has not cooperated with investigators, accused ICE of destroying evidence intentionally or through gross negligence, and said the driver fled the scene before the vehicle could be impounded. Parra Hernandez has lived in the U.S. for more than 30 years without authorization, according to the group helping his family.

Teare is also investigating the July fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo by an ICE officer, which set off protests in Houston. DHS has said Salgado Araujo weaponized his vehicle. ICE did not immediately comment on the indictment, and the case may raise questions about whether federal agents can be prosecuted by local authorities.

stories.headline: Update: Tech Stocks Fall for Second Day as Intel Plunges and AI Spending Fears Grow
stories.summary:
Tech stocks fell for a second straight day Friday as investors worried about the hundreds of billions of dollars companies are spending on artificial intelligence. The Nasdaq sank more than 3.5%. Intel shares dropped as much as 30%, putting more than $130 billion of its market value at risk, a day after Alphabet lost over $500 billion in value.

Intel's finance chief, David Zinsner, said the company does not expect to generate more cash than it spends this year and forecast fourth-quarter revenue below expectations. He said the PC slowdown should last at least through the first half of next year, even as Intel plans to raise equipment spending. Amazon shares fell as much as 6% in overnight trading after earnings missed expectations and spending rose six-fold over three months, and were down about 1.6% in Friday trading. The company has committed to $220 billion in spending this year.

Reddit fell 26% after weaker daily user figures and a warning that Google's AI-driven search is cutting referral traffic. Roblox dropped nearly 20% on lower daily active users. Alphabet slipped a further 2.2% after Thursday's 12% decline, which followed its disclosure that AI summaries are affecting search advertising revenue.

Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon and Microsoft have committed to about $800.6 billion in combined spending in 2026. Analysts questioned whether earnings can justify the outlays, and the selloff has revived fears of an AI bubble.

stories.headline: G20 Family Photo Cancelled After European Diplomats Refuse to Pose With Russia's Lavrov
stories.summary:
The United States cancelled the traditional group photo at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Atlanta on Friday after European diplomats refused to stand alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov. Two officials confirmed the cancellation to the BBC. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is hosting the gathering.

A British official said the UK has a longstanding policy against direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and would not change it. A US official said the photo was dropped after some delegations proved unwilling to participate, and that Washington chose to keep the focus on substantive discussions rather than let a ceremonial moment become a distraction. Ukraine, not a G20 member, was not invited, though it has attended similar meetings in recent years.

The episode reflects a split over Russia policy. US-Russia relations have partially thawed as President Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel, aimed at lowering fuel prices before the midterms. Trump says suspending sanctions keeps Moscow at the negotiating table, while Ukraine's President Zelensky called the deal a gift to Putin and an investment in prolonging the war.

Ties between Washington and Kyiv have been tense this month over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. Russia has meanwhile intensified missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other cities, while agreeing to a US call to resume peace talks.

stories.headline: Update: Vance Calls for Investigation of Second 'Dan Sullivan' Candidacy as DOJ Issues Subpoenas
stories.summary:
Vice President JD Vance said Thursday that the alleged Democratic scheme to place a second Dan Sullivan on Alaska's Senate ballot should be investigated, arguing that deliberately deceiving voters should be illegal. Speaking at a Fox News town hall in Fort Worth, Texas, he said he is not a legal expert but that a candidate seeking to mislead and defraud voters should face consequences if current law does not already cover it.

The remarks come as the Justice Department intensifies its criminal investigation into the candidacy of Daniel J. Sullivan, whose name closely resembles that of Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan. DOJ sources told Fox News more than 30 subpoenas were issued in the previous 24 hours. Vance also criticized Democratic nominee Mary Peltola for avoiding questions on the matter and urged Alaskans to vote for the incumbent.

Peltola's campaign has denied involvement in recruiting the similarly named candidate. The New York Times earlier reported that campaign operatives helped recruit spoiler candidates, and the Alaska governor and House Oversight have opened probes. Democrats have criticized the escalating federal involvement days before the Nov. 3 election, while Republicans say the matter involves voter deception.

stories.headline: Novaya Gazeta, Russia's Last Major Independent Newspaper, Shuts Down Under Government Pressure
stories.summary:
Novaya Gazeta, for three decades one of Russia's most prominent independent news outlets, announced it is closing and accused the authorities of murdering the newspaper. "They've killed us," read a statement on its website. "The Russian authorities and Russian special services have forced the paper to stop its work."

The paper received an eviction order and, at the same time, the system that let it collect reader donations was disabled, leaving it with no way to fund operations. It had already lost its licence and had its website blocked, and several journalists were labelled "foreign agents." Earlier this year police searched its offices, investigative journalist Oleg Roldugin was arrested on a charge of unlawful access to computerised information, and editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov was questioned and had his home searched.

The outlet, co-founded by a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, said six journalists connected with it were killed for doing their jobs, including Anna Politkovskaya, shot dead 20 years ago this month. Its statement said human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in Russia and that "having personal convictions is now state treason."

Pressure on independent media has grown since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, when new laws punishing dissent and criticism of the war were adopted. Readers had used VPNs to get around the blocking. The Kremlin has not been quoted in the available coverage.

stories.headline: Trump Reinstates Iowa and Kansas Rallies a Day After Cancelling Them as Senate Races Tighten
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump will hold in-person rallies in Iowa and Kansas this weekend after all, a day after the Republican National Committee said he would instead hold tele-rallies. Sources told The Hill, Washington Examiner and other outlets that the events are back on. The reversal came five days before Tuesday's midterm elections, and the original change had fueled speculation about why he was scaling back travel.

The Senate races in both states are considered toss-ups. An Emerson College poll shows Democrat Adam Hamilton at 48.7% to Republican Sen. Roger Marshall's 45.2% in Kansas. Marshall had said he was doing so well that Trump had better places to spend his time. A Republican-aligned source said Trump loves his supporters and wanted to extend his time on the trail.

Elsewhere, the Cook Political Report shifted a dozen more House races toward Democrats and now forecasts more than 218 seats leaning Democratic. It also moved Senate races in Nebraska and Florida toward challengers while still favoring Republican incumbents. A CNN poll across four Senate races found Democrats well-positioned in Michigan and Texas, with no clear leader in Maine or Kansas. Republicans argue their base turns out most when Trump is engaged personally, while Democrats point to his low approval ratings and affordability concerns as dragging down incumbents.

Early voting is far above the last midterm, with nearly 45 million ballots already cast according to ABC News and an Associated Press analysis.

stories.headline: Alphabet Loses $500 Billion in Value as AI Search Cuts Into Ad Sales; Tech Stocks Slide
stories.summary:
Alphabet lost just over $500 billion in market value on Thursday after disclosing that its own AI-powered search features are eating into its traditional search advertising revenue. Its total market capitalization fell to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before, and shares dropped more than 12% to a six-month low. Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said the company's conversational "AI mode" is cannibalizing ad income tied to traditional search queries, though he said he felt "very good about our trajectory."

Third-quarter revenue rose 25% from a year earlier to $127.6 billion, but the figure fell short of analyst expectations, particularly in advertising. Amazon shares fell about 6% in after-hours trading after it reported 11% sales growth to $201 billion alongside negative cash flow of $42 billion, with spending up roughly six-fold over three months. Chief executive Andy Jassy said the company sees the chance to build two businesses that could each reach $1 trillion, pointing to its custom chips and its Bedrock AI platform. Intel also fell after its results.

The selloff renewed fears that the AI investment boom could unravel. The New York Times reported the S&P 500 is on track for a small monthly loss, with the broader market holding up better than the AI-heavy names that carry outsized weight in the index. Asian markets also fell Friday, with SK Hynix down more than 6% and SoftBank down 4.7%, while news of the Binance hack added to the pressure on sentiment.

Former Google advertising chief Kim Scott told the BBC the company would "rather eat its own lunch than allow someone else to eat their lunch," describing the spending as a long-term bet on AI. Microsoft, Amazon and Google have all said they will keep spending heavily, while investors worry about the effect on growth in their core businesses.

stories.headline: Update: Comey Asks Judge to Block Third Criminal Case; DOJ Subpoenas California Election Officials
stories.summary:
Lawyers for former FBI director James Comey are scheduled to ask a federal judge on Friday to block the Justice Department from pursuing its third criminal case against him, which concerns the alleged leaking of defense information. They argue the case is invalid on its face because it was not presented to a federal grand jury within the statute of limitations. The leak matter was twice investigated previously without action being taken.

Comey, a longtime critic of President Trump who was fired by him early in his first term, has frequently been a target of Republican criticism. Supporters of the prosecution say the department is entitled to pursue credible leak allegations, while Comey's defenders and many Democrats describe the cases as politically driven retaliation against a presidential adversary.

Separately, ABC News reported that the Justice Department has issued grand jury subpoenas to local election officials in California as part of an investigation into the state's voter rolls. A federal judge this week blocked a separate DOJ effort to sequester ballots from more than 20,000 suspected noncitizen voters on California's rolls. The administration says it is working to ensure roll accuracy, while California officials and Democrats call the moves an effort to undermine confidence in the vote days before the Nov. 3 midterms.

The hearings come as Trump makes a final in-person push in Florida, scheduled to speak in Daytona Beach on Friday evening to support Sen. Ashley Moody. The Republican National Committee said he scrapped weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa in favor of tele-rallies.

stories.headline: Christa Pike Says She Is in Constant Pain After Failed Execution
stories.summary:
Death row inmate Christa Pike released her first public statement since her botched execution in September, saying she has been in pain every moment since. Her legal team posted the statement on social media Friday. "My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak," she said, adding that the pain is also in her mind and soul.

Pike, 50, survived two lethal injections of pentobarbital that left her in critical condition. She was discharged from hospital at the end of last month and returned to the prison where she has spent 30 years. Her lawyers have said she suffered pneumonia, significant arm swelling and difficulty swallowing. She is believed to be the only person to survive an attempted lethal injection execution.

"I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger," she said, "but healing is not the same as being okay." Pike was convicted of the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom she and then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp beat, tortured and killed at the age of 18. Shipp avoided the death penalty because he was a minor.

The statement is likely to renew debate over lethal injection protocols and whether a second execution attempt should be allowed. Supporters of capital punishment stress the severity of the crime, while opponents cite the failed procedure as evidence of the method's flaws.

stories.headline: Three Killed in Midair Helicopter Collision Near Oregon Airport
stories.summary:
Two helicopters collided midair near McMinnville Municipal Airport in Oregon on Thursday afternoon, killing all three people aboard, officials said. A Robinson R22 and an Airbus helicopter crashed in a field next to a highway, according to the sheriff's office.

The victims were identified as Maddie Aasbo, a 22-year-old flight instructor from Texas, and a student pilot from the United Kingdom who has not been publicly named while authorities work with the consulate and the FBI to notify relatives. The sole occupant of the other aircraft was identified as Tyler Delane Sturdevant, 38, of Newberg, Oregon.

One of the aircraft was operated by Jerry Trimble Helicopters, a flight school based at the airport, which said it was deeply saddened and is cooperating with investigators. The Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board are leading the investigation, and the cause was not immediately clear. Authorities asked the public to avoid the area during the response.

stories.headline: Update: Binance Hack Put at $6.3 Billion, Half of Assets Frozen as Analysts Point to North Korean Group
stories.summary:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said it has been hit by a hack totaling about $6.3 billion, up from the roughly $5.7 billion figure initially under investigation. The company said about half of the stolen assets have been frozen, but a substantial share remains in the hands of the attackers.

Two blockchain analytics firms have attributed the incident to a North Korean hacking unit, although no group has claimed responsibility. Binance did not directly answer questions about possible links to North Korea. Pyongyang-linked hackers have been blamed for several large crypto thefts in recent years, and U.S. authorities have said such proceeds help fund the country's weapons programs.

The scale of the theft would make it among the largest in the history of digital assets. It raises questions about the security of centralized exchanges and the exposure of customers who hold funds on them. Binance has not detailed how the attackers gained access or what it will do to reimburse affected users.

Investigators and analytics firms are continuing to trace the movement of the stolen funds, and further freezes or recoveries are possible as exchanges and law enforcement coordinate. The incident is also likely to draw regulatory attention to the industry's custody and security practices.

stories.headline: Update: Supreme Court Lets New Hampshire Bar Student IDs for Voting, Curbs Judges' Power Over Deportation Cases
stories.summary:
The Supreme Court ruled 8-1 to allow New Hampshire to block student IDs as a valid form of voter identification. The decision lets the state's restriction stand just days before the November 3 midterm elections.

Separately, in a ruling stemming from the Fifth Circuit, the court held that immigration judges lack the power to shelve deportation cases, a decision that sharply curtails the ability of judges to free undocumented immigrants from the removal process. Supporters of stricter immigration enforcement have framed the ruling as restoring the intended limits of immigration court authority.

Voting rights advocates have long argued that excluding student IDs makes it harder for young voters to cast ballots, while supporters of such laws say they protect election integrity and ensure consistent identification standards. Immigrant advocates warned that the deportation ruling removes a tool judges used to manage caseloads and spare people with strong equities from removal, while enforcement proponents said it ends a form of administrative discretion Congress never granted.

The court's docket also includes a dispute over Colorado preschool benefits, in which a mother says her family was denied $12,000 because she chose a Catholic school, a claim she describes as religious discrimination.

stories.headline: Update: Russian Drone Strike on Dnipro Rail Station Kills at Least 14 as Ukraine Truce Around Oleshky Holds
stories.summary:
A Russian jet-powered drone hit a crowded platform at the main railway station in Dnipro, killing at least 14 people and wounding at least 14 others, including an 11-year-old boy, regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said. A passenger train bound for Zaporizhzhia was at the platform. Russia has not commented publicly and denies deliberately targeting civilians.

Elsewhere, two 15-year-old girls were killed in a missile attack on Chernihiv, with at least 25 others injured, and three people were killed and 28 injured in a drone attack on Kremenchuk that hit homes and a school. Ukraine declared a day of mourning for Dnipro and Chernihiv on Friday. President Volodymyr Zelensky called for further U.S., European and G7 sanctions and criticized an earlier deal between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin that eased some sanctions and allowed U.S. imports of Russian diesel.

The strikes came during a fragile, U.S.-brokered temporary ceasefire tied to an evacuation of civilians from Russian-occupied Oleshky, an effort championed by First Lady Melania Trump. Ukraine's ombudsman said the truce was holding into a third day, and Kherson residents have enjoyed their first quiet in years. The pause is due to end Sunday, and Ukrainian officials fear Russia is using it to reinforce positions ahead of a renewed assault on Kherson.

Moscow, meanwhile, said 613 Ukrainian drones were launched toward the Moscow region overnight as it hosted the Russia-Africa Summit.

stories.headline: Democrats Prepare Corporate Subpoenas as Justice Department Deploys 1,000 Election Monitors
stories.summary:
With Democrats favored to gain ground in the midterms, party members are preparing investigations and subpoenas aimed at corporate executives who embraced President Trump after his 2024 victory with large investment pledges. Axios reports that CEOs who tied their fortunes to the administration could spend the last two years of Trump's term defending their dealings under oath. Republicans and allies of the administration have generally cast such probes as politically motivated.

Separately, local election officials are raising concerns as the Justice Department deploys 1,000 monitors to polling sites. The department has framed monitoring as routine oversight of election law compliance, while some local officials worry about possible intimidation at the polls.

In a related legal development, U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns ruled Thursday that the Trump administration's definition of "medically frail" for Medicaid purposes, drawn from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, is "contrary to law." He issued a temporary injunction on states having to determine medical frailty. The administration is expected to face questions about whether it will appeal.

A POLITICO poll also shows the business community has work to do to win over a wary public, as the midterms arrive on November 3.
